conventions.convention: Hamiltonians are finite-dimensional complex self-adjoint endomorphisms; U_H(t) has spectral coefficients exp(−itλ) for real t. On the zero space the empty spectral sum is the identity.
Graph weights are symmetric and nonnegative; loops count once in row sums. L_+ = D−A, L_- = A−D. Normalized adjacency is defined only when every degree is positive.
A quantum-walk state requires a nonzero space and a unit representative of a pure-state ray; changing its global phase leaves the output ray unchanged.
The root inner product is linear first; a bra acts by z ↦ ⟨z,y⟩, so |x⟩⟨y| sends z to ⟨z,y⟩x.
The hypercube dimension n may be zero; the empty tensor register is C with one empty-word basis label and identity empty tensor map.

Matrix descriptions supply no implementation. Preparation, evolution, measurement, oracle access, gates, description bits, precision, and classical construction are separately declared and charged; controlled and inverse access are separate capabilities.
Complete-graph search uses N ≥ 2, injective m-bit labels, adjacency extended by zero outside the active label subspace, H = −A/N−P_w, and time π√N/2. Unused measured strings return FAIL.

load_bearing.statement: Let H be a self-adjoint endomorphism of a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space V. For real t,s, U_H(0)=I_V, U_H(t)*U_H(t)=I_V, U_H(t+s)=U_H(t)U_H(s), and U_H′(t)=−iHU_H(t). Moreover, U_H is the unique differentiable map Y:R→End(V) satisfying Y′(t)=−iHY(t) and Y(0)=I_V.

A Hamiltonian-access contract separately declares the input representation, implementation or certified unitary simulator, preparation and measurement stages, and their query, gate, description-bit, precision, and classical-construction costs. A matrix description alone supplies no efficient evolution, controlled call, inverse call, or zero-cost operation.

For a unit vector φ in a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with finite orthonormal basis (e_y), basis measurement gives p_φ(y)=|⟨φ,e_y⟩|² and Σ_y p_φ(y)=1. In particular this applies to φ=U_H(t)ψ for self-adjoint H, real t, and unit ψ.

For every integer n ≥ 0, H=(1/√2)[[1,1],[1,−1]] is unitary and H tensor n applied to e_(0^n) equals 2^(−n/2) Σ_x e_x. The preparation uses exactly n one-qubit H gates when H is primitive; otherwise implementation and synthesis costs must be supplied.

For a unit input ψ and unitary U,W on a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with finite orthonormal basis, if ρ ≥ 0 and ||W−U||op ≤ ρ, then every basis-outcome probability satisfies |p_W(y)−p_U(y)| ≤ 2ρ.
For every integer n ≥ 0, the hypercube-transfer algorithm evolves e_(0^n) to U_(A_n)(π/2)e_(0^n)=(−i)^n e_(1^n), and measurement outputs 1^n with probability one, including the empty word when n=0.

For every N ≥ 2, marked label w, and encoded complete-graph instance with the supplied exact uniform preparation, evolution under H=−A/N−P_w at t=π√N/2 yields the marked basis ray with probability exactly 1. Replacing it by a unitary V with ||V−U_H(t)||op ≤ ρ for ρ ≥ 0 gives marked-label probability at least 1−2ρ.

published_dependencies.used_for: Self-adjoint and normal operator definitions and the implication self-adjoint ⇒ normal.
Adjoint identities with the linear-first inner-product convention.
Linearity, conjugate symmetry, positive definiteness, and induced norm.
Finite orthonormal eigenbases for normal operators.
Finite spectral functional calculus defining evolution.
Exponential power series and exp(0)=1.
Natural powers, including 0^0=1.
Factorial conventions, nonvanishing, and 0!=1.
Scalar exponential addition law and agreement with the real exponential.
Euler formula, conjugate phases, and unit modulus at imaginary arguments.
Differentiating spectral coefficients and the uniqueness integrating factor.
A differentiable real component with zero derivative is constant, after checking continuity.
Real product rules used to derive the complex product rule.
Computing the basis-measurement trace in an ordered basis.
Basis expansions, probability normalization, and bounds on individual coordinates.
Bounding the output-vector difference by operator-norm error.
Existence and attainment of the finite-dimensional operator-norm maximum.
Unitary norm preservation.
Complex modulus as the Euclidean norm of real coordinates.
The triangle inequality used in the probability-stability estimate.
Exact phases at π/2 and π and integer π shifts.
Determining the least nonnegative ray-transfer times in the normalization counterexample.
Power-series evaluations bounding sin(1) and cos(1).
Consecutive-partial-sum bounds proving the sign-convention witness has distinct probabilities.

seams_checked.note: The access and resource items retain full-list uniform generation and separate gate, oracle, description, precision, and classical costs.
Ordered computational bases, factorwise tensor maps, and the one-dimensional empty tensor register agree with the suppliers.
Walk states use unit representatives of rays on nonzero spaces; the measurement proof uses the supplied rank-one density-projector result.
The measurement proof constructs a finite basis PVM and evaluates its trace law to derive squared-coordinate probabilities.
Dirac outer products and amplitudes preserve the root linear-first pairing; marked projectors have the stated coordinate action.
Controlled and inverse calls remain explicitly supplied capabilities with separately declared costs.
The marked predicate is a total XOR oracle, including unused labels; its availability does not grant continuous-time marked-projector evolution.
The complete-graph example uses the declared Dirac projector convention and ordered orthonormal coordinates.
Simulation definitions and product-formula citations use finite self-adjoint evolution, its derivative, unitarity, composition law, and uniqueness with the same negative exponential sign.
The polynomial target exp(−iαtx) gives exp(−itλ) on an H eigenvector. Small-time and sparse lower-bound citations retain finite Hermitian unitarity and derivative hypotheses.

The parameter-shift item uses spectral evolution for its self-adjoint involution; sparse-resource substitution cites finite Hermitian unitarity and differentiation without claiming implementation costs from them.
Discretized simulation uses finite Hermitian frozen-term evolutions and separately supplied term providers; the citation does not treat the time-dependent path as a single constant-H exponential.
